Variants.Content: Naples lay on a broad bay under the shadow of Vesuvius, and it served as the mainland anchor of the Kingdom of Sicily. Frederick II had founded its university in 1224, and the city produced trained jurists and royal administrators loyal to the Hohenstaufen crown. Its harbour shipped grain, timber and oil from the Campanian plain to vessels bound for the Levant and the Adriatic. Merchants from Amalfi and Genoa brought cloth and spices in return, and royal customs houses taxed every cargo. Because the court depended on that trade for income, the crown guarded the port closely, and any disruption to the sea lanes reached the royal treasury within weeks.

For a lord, Naples is a question of the grain fleet. Every cargo that clears the gulf pays toll to the crown, and every castle on the coast guards a share of that revenue. Lords who hold land near Castel dell'Ovo or the southern anchorages watch the ships closely, because a bribed customs clerk or a blockaded roadstead can cut their rents in a single season.
